catalog_quote: [Wikipedia, Tone] As a tone-language, Pech has two to three distinctive pitch-levels: high tone (á, é, í, ó, ú) low tone (à, è, ì, ò, ù), and sometimes, extra low tone. This lower than normal tone is rare, though it occurs particularly with the suffix ''-rih''. Tones distinguish between lexical items and inflectional types [Wikipedia, Stress] Pech has primary and secondary levels of stress, which are not distinctive. They rely on the underlying marked tone and stem syllables. Primary stress tends to occur in the last syllable of the stem. Primary and secondary stress are also related to inflectional suffixes. ... [Chamoreau 2021 fn. 2] In Holt's transcription, the accents indicate types of tone, and the tilde indicates nasalization. ... tone_statements.citation: Pache, Matthias J. 2018. Contributions to Chibchan historical linguistics. PhD dissertation, Universiteit Leiden. (section 2.3.20 'Pech', pp. 452-458; 2.4 Proto-Chibchan phonology)
tone_statements.quote: Two or three pitch levels are contrastive in Pech, namely high tone (V́), low tone (V̀), and possibly an extra low tone, with little evidence for the latter, however. Pitch-distinctions can have both an inflectional function and distinguish between lexical items (Holt 1999a: 18–9). These tones occur in “certain marked syllables”; tone may spread via assimilation or prosodic tonal patterns to “unmarked syllables” (ibid.: 18).

tone_statements.quote: La lengua pesh pertenece a la familia chibcha. Su sistema numérico es decimal. Fonológicamente es tonal, significa que una misma palabra puede cambiar de significado según el tono alto (’), medio (no se marca) o bajo (`) con que se pronuncie: óh ‘caña’, oh(a) ‘correr’, òk(a) ‘dormir’ [...] En la lengua pesh no hay acento fonético o prosódico, como en las demás, ya que existe el tono, por esto, en una misma palabra pueden concurrir los tres tonos apuntados arriba
tone_statements.translation: The Pesh language belongs to the Chibchan family. Its numeral system is decimal. Phonologically it is tonal, meaning that one and the same word can change meaning according to the high ('), mid (unmarked) or low (`) tone with which it is pronounced: óh 'cane', oh(a) 'to run', òk(a) 'to sleep' [...] In Pesh there is no phonetic or prosodic stress accent, as in the other languages, since there is tone; hence the three tones noted above can co-occur in a single word

sources.quote: Two or three pitch levels are contrastive in Pech, namely high tone (V́), low tone (V̀), and possibly an extra low tone, with little evidence for the latter, however. Pitch-distinctions can have both an inflectional function and distinguish between lexical items (Holt 1999a: 18–9). sources.note: Secondhand (from Holt 1999a: 18-19): two or three contrastive pitch levels - high, low and a doubtful extra-low; tone distinguishes lexical items and inflectional types; tones sit on 'marked syllables' and spread to unmarked ones; stress (primary/secondary) largely predictable from underlying tone. Also (p.515) lists Pech among the Chibchan languages with tone, declines to reconstruct Proto-Chibchan tone, and (p.113, p.218) tentatively links Pech low tone to a Proto-Chibchan final glottal stop.

sources.note: Secondhand overview (no source cited): Pesh is tonal with THREE tones - high (acute), mid (unmarked) and low (grave) - illustrated óh 'cane' / oh(a) 'run' / òk(a) 'sleep'; says Pesh has no phonetic/prosodic stress accent because it has tone, all three tones can co-occur in one word; practical alphabet writes high and low tone, mid unwritten. Conflicts with Holt's two-level (+rare extra-low) analysis.
